PROJECT HIGHLIGHT

Clothes dryers may be a major source of plastic microfiber pollution — the most common form of microplastic pollution globally and the type most often ingested by humans and wildlife. This project provided the first estimates of how much microplastic pollution dryers release during real-world use and assessed whether add-on filters offer a practical solution for reducing this pollution.

 

PROJECT SUMMARY

Modern textiles often include plastic fibers, which shed from clothes and spread into the environment. Plastic microfibers are now the most widespread form of microplastic pollution reported globally, as well as the type most commonly ingested by humans and wildlife. While many researchers once assumed that water from washing machines was the major source, recent studies suggest that air vented from clothes dryers may be a bigger culprit.

This project investigated that hypothesis through residential and commercial sampling in the San Francisco Bay region. The research team collected dryer exhaust samples from 19 volunteer households and a shared dormitory laundry room at California State University, East Bay. A public survey was distributed widely to gather information about how frequently Bay Area households did laundry. The team also tested three types of add-on dryer filters in a controlled laboratory setting and assessed how well they captured microfibers.

Study findings indicate that measurable amounts of lint containing both plastic and natural fibers are being vented outdoors from each laundry load. Early estimates suggest that dryer emissions are a major source of microfibers in rainwater runoff to the San Francisco Bay. Results on add-on dryer filters show that these devices can significantly reduce microfiber emissions, presenting a practical solution. Based on the collected data, the research team built a model to estimate the fiber loads reaching San Francisco Bay. While focused on the San Francisco Bay, the findings are widely useful across North American urban areas where vented drying units are common.
